subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: The primary objective of state 'Sunshine Laws' and the federal Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) is to:
options: Ensure public funds are invested in renewable energy.
Maximize the speed of public procurement transactions.
Guarantee that the public has access to the records and proceedings of their government to promote transparency.
Protect vendors from having their contracts scrutinized by competitors.
questions.explain: Sunshine Laws and FOIA mandates transparency by ensuring that the public has a fundamental right to access government records and observe meetings, functioning as a check on government operations.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: Under typical public records laws, if a government agency wishes to withhold a requested procurement document from a citizen, who bears the legal burden of proof to justify the withholding?
options: The citizen requesting the document.
The government agency holding the document.
The vendor whose name is on the document.
The state's attorney general automatically.
questions.explain: Under FOIA and state equivalents, there is a presumption of disclosure. The government agency bears the burden of proof to demonstrate that a specific legal exemption applies to justify withholding the record.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: A competitor files a public records request for a winning vendor's proposal one day after the bid opening, but before the evaluation committee has made an award recommendation. Most jurisdictions will handle this request by:
options: Releasing the proposals immediately, as all public records must be released within 24 hours.
Delaying the release under an exemption that protects active solicitations until a notice of intent to award is issued.
Denying the request permanently, as vendor proposals are always classified.
Charging the competitor a mandatory $1,000 fee to release the documents.
questions.explain: Most state public records laws include an exemption for active solicitations. Proposals are typically shielded from public release during the evaluation phase to maintain a fair competitive environment, becoming public only after an award decision (or notice of intent) is made.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: If a FOIA request demands thousands of pages of procurement data that will require a week of staff time to compile and copy, how does the law typically direct the agency to handle the costs?
options: The agency must fulfill the request entirely for free, regardless of staff time.
The agency can deny the request entirely as an unreasonable burden.
The agency may charge a reasonable, legally defined fee for the labor and materials required to fulfill the request.
The agency should tell the requester to physically come and sort through the agency's filing cabinets.
questions.explain: Most public records laws allow agencies to charge reasonable fees (as defined by statute) to cover the actual costs of extensive search, review, and duplication, particularly when fulfilling the request requires significant staff labor.

questions.q: Are personal notes taken by an evaluation committee member during a vendor presentation considered public records subject to disclosure?
options: No, because they were handwritten.
Yes, if they were created in the course of conducting public business and used to make an agency decision.
No, personal notes are explicitly exempt under the federal FOIA.
Yes, but only if the vendor explicitly requests them.
questions.explain: In many jurisdictions, personal notes taken by public employees during the course of official duties—especially those used to score or evaluate a public contract—are considered public records subject to disclosure.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: Which of the following documents is most likely to be completely EXEMPT from disclosure under freedom of information or public records laws?
options: A fully executed contract with a janitorial service.
The scoring matrix utilized by an evaluation team.
Draft internal security plans detailing vulnerabilities in the agency's cybersecurity infrastructure.
An email from the procurement director setting up a meeting time.
questions.explain: Documents that reveal critical security vulnerabilities, infrastructure weaknesses, or active security protocols are broadly exempt from public records laws to protect public safety and prevent cyber/physical attacks.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: A citizen submits a FOIA request asking the procurement officer to 'explain why Vendor X was chosen.' The officer does not have any existing document that explicitly writes out this explanation, though the score sheets show Vendor X scored highest. Is the officer required to type out a new explanatory document to fulfill the FOIA request?
options: Yes, FOIA requires government employees to explain their actions in writing upon request.
No, FOIA laws generally require the production of existing records, not the creation of new records or explanations.
Yes, but only if the citizen pays a consulting fee.
No, because evaluating vendors is considered a state secret.
questions.explain: Freedom of Information laws require agencies to provide access to existing records. They do not obligate government officials to create new documents, answer written interrogatories, or write explanations that do not currently exist.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: An agency receives a public records request for emails between the City Manager and the agency's Legal Counsel discussing the legal strategy for an upcoming breach of contract lawsuit against a vendor. These documents are generally:
options: Released immediately because all emails are public records.
Exempt from disclosure under the Attorney-Client Privilege or work-product doctrine.
Released, but only to the vendor being sued.
Destroyed immediately.
questions.explain: Communications between a government entity and its legal counsel made for the purpose of obtaining or providing legal advice—especially regarding active litigation—are protected by attorney-client privilege and exempt from public disclosure.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: When fulfilling a public records request, an agency discovers an email chain between the buyer and a vendor. Half of the email discusses lunch plans, and the other half contains sensitive trade secrets. Under FOIA principles, what is the correct handling?
options: Destroy the entire email so the trade secrets are protected.
Release the entire email because personal lunch plans void trade secret protections.
Apply the principle of 'severability' by redacting the trade secrets and releasing the remainder of the email.
Ask the vendor to write a new email that doesn't contain the trade secrets.
questions.explain: The principle of severability (or partial disclosure) requires that if a record contains both exempt and non-exempt material, the agency must sever (redact) the exempt portion and disclose the non-exempt portion.
